text: What does a cigarette do to me?

args.label: Nicotine (one cigarette)

targets.effect: Smoke irritates airway lining; nicotine absorbed through air sacs
Triggers dopamine release; brief alertness and reward
Faster beat, tighter vessels, higher blood pressure
Clear nicotine and cotinine into urine

args.source: Benowitz et al. 2009, Handb Exp Pharmacol: ~1-1.5 mg absorbed per cigarette, half-life ~2 h, Vd ~2.6 L/kg

args.label: Cigarette
args.source: Own estimate from Benowitz 2009 and Cryer 1976: one cigarette raises heart rate about 10 bpm and blood pressure 5-10 mmHg for about 30 min

feelings.label: Buzzed
feelings.cause: Nicotine releasing dopamine in the brain

feelings.label: Scratchy
feelings.cause: Hot smoke irritating the airway lining

stops.label: Lungs
stops.say: Smoke reaches the air sacs; nicotine and carbon monoxide cross into the blood.

stops.label: Heart
stops.say: Blood carries nicotine straight to the left side of the heart.

stops.label: Brain
stops.say: Within seconds nicotine reaches the brain and releases dopamine.

stops.label: Liver
stops.say: The liver slowly turns nicotine into cotinine.

steps.title: Smoke hits the air sacs
steps.say: As an example, one cigarette now. Hot smoke irritates your airway lining, and in the tiny air sacs nicotine and carbon monoxide slip straight into your blood.

composed.caption: Smoke entering an air sac
composed.basis: Textbook picture of smoke absorption in the alveoli (Benowitz 2009); amounts are illustrative

steps.title: Carbon monoxide steals oxygen seats
steps.say: Carbon monoxide grips red blood cells far more tightly than oxygen does, so for a few hours your blood carries a little less oxygen.

composed.caption: Carbon monoxide crowding out oxygen
composed.basis: Haemoglobin binds CO about 200 times more tightly than oxygen (standard physiology); amounts are illustrative

steps.title: Seconds later, the brain
steps.say: Blood from the lungs reaches your brain in about ten seconds. Nicotine unlocks receptors that release dopamine, the reward signal, which is the brief buzz and the hook.

composed.caption: Nicotine releasing dopamine at a nerve ending
composed.basis: Nicotinic receptors on dopamine neurons in the reward pathway (Benowitz 2010, NEJM); amounts are illustrative

steps.title: Your heart speeds up
steps.say: Nicotine also releases adrenaline, so your heart goes from about 78 to 88 beats a minute and vessels tighten, pushing blood pressure up.

steps.title: Short buzz, slow clearing
steps.say: Within half an hour your pulse settles and the buzz is gone, which is why smokers want another. Your liver clears nicotine slowly, so half is still in you two hours later.

steps.title: What stays behind
steps.say: Tar settles on the airway lining and its cleaning hairs slow down. One cigarette heals; years of them leave the damage behind cough, lung disease and cancer.

closeup.basis: Own illustration; chronic airway inflammation in smokers is described in GOLD COPD reports

lines.text: Nicotine reaches your brain within seconds and releases dopamine, a brief buzz that hooks you.
Your pulse would jump from about 78 to 88, then settle within half an hour.
Smoke irritates your airways, and you may feel a scratchy throat. Half the nicotine stays two hours.
